title: Canada Launches Data Page Revealing Full Scope of Permanent Residence Admissions
excerpt: A new IRCC web page confirms that actual planned PR admissions for 2026–2027 total 908,000 — far exceeding the headline levels plan target of 380,000 per year — by accounting for two one-time initiatives previously excluded from official targets.
body:
• IRCC launched a new web page on July 21 showing monthly PR admissions data, separating levels plan admissions from two "one-time initiatives" for protected persons and in-Canada workers.
  • Canada's actual planned PR admissions for 2026–2027 total 908,000 — an average of 454,000 per year — well above the 380,000 annual target in the levels plan.
  • As of May 2026, 128,900 new permanent residents have been admitted, with one-time initiative PRs accounting for about 14.4% of the total.
  • The move follows a July 21 update to the government's backlog page, which now distinguishes applications slated for processing this year from those waitlisted for future years.

New Data Page Goes Live

Canada's immigration department has taken a notable step toward greater transparency on permanent residence admissions. On July 21, 2026, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) launched a new web page titled "Understanding permanent residence numbers in Canada," providing a monthly breakdown of PR admissions that separates standard levels plan admissions from those processed under two separate one-time initiatives.

https://x.com/canadavisa_com/status/2079944104406864067

The page makes explicit what was first disclosed in Budget 2025 last November: the 380,000 annual PR admissions target set in the 2026–2028 Immigration Levels Plan does not include admissions under two supplementary programs — a protected persons initiative covering up to 115,000 individuals and an in-Canada workers initiative covering up to 33,000 — both running across 2026 and 2027.

When these initiatives are factored in, the cumulative total of planned PR admissions for 2026–2027 rises to 908,000, averaging 454,000 per year — roughly 19% higher than the headline target suggests.

What the Numbers Show

According to the new data page, Canada admitted 128,900 new permanent residents between January and May 2026. Of these, one-time initiative admissions accounted for about 14.4% of the total.

The in-Canada workers initiative has admitted 9,100 PRs through May 2026, reaching 46% of its annual target of 20,000. This pathway fast-tracks workers already contributing to Canadian communities in in-demand sectors, with a focus on those who have lived in smaller communities for at least two years and applied through programs such as the Provincial Nominee Program, Atlantic Immigration Program, and Rural Community Immigration Pilot.

The protected persons initiative has admitted 9,300 PRs, hitting 20% of its 46,000 annual target. This initiative processes applications from people with recognized protected status who cannot safely return to their country of origin.

"We have committed to returning immigration to sustainable levels, stabilizing the number of new permanent residents each year to less than 1% of our total population beyond 2027 with a focus on giving permanent residence to people already living in, working in, and contributing to our country."

— IRCC, Understanding permanent residence numbers in Canada

Backlog Page Also Updated

The new admissions page arrived alongside an update to IRCC's application backlog page, which as of July 21 began presenting a breakdown of PR applications slated for processing in the current year versus those waitlisted for future years to conform with annual admissions targets under the levels plan.

This dual update comes days after the federal government closed the intake for new Parents and Grandparents Program (PGP) sponsorship applications on July 15, reporting 50,900 PGP PR applications already in its inventory — against a target of just 15,000 PGP admissions per year for 2026 through 2028.

Separately, IRCC's July 7 processing times update showed wait times declining by one to two months for Canadian Experience Class, base Provincial Nominee Program, and Parent and Grandparent applicants, according to CIC News.

What This Means for Indian Applicants

India consistently ranks as the top source country for Canadian permanent residence, with Indian nationals making up the largest share of Express Entry invitees and Provincial Nominee Program candidates. The transparency push is directly relevant to hundreds of thousands of Indians in Canada's PR pipeline, many of whom are temporary residents — international graduates and skilled workers — seeking to transition to permanent status.

The in-Canada workers initiative, in particular, targets exactly this demographic: temporary residents already working in Canadian communities who applied through provincial and regional programs. With that pathway already 46% toward its 2026 target by May, eligible Indian workers in smaller communities stand to benefit from the accelerated processing.

A Pattern of Parallel Transparency

The new PR admissions page follows the same format as the "Understanding student and temporary worker numbers in Canada" page that the government published in August 2025. Both pages aim to provide clearer data on immigration categories where headline numbers do not capture the full picture.

CIC News noted a parallel with Budget 2025's fiscal reporting, which introduced a new framework splitting government spending into "day-to-day operating spending" versus "capital investments" — a categorization that economist Jim Stanford of the Centre for Future Work called "utterly arbitrary." Whether the immigration data page faces similar scrutiny over its presentation of the numbers remains to be seen.

For now, the dashboard gives applicants and the public a clearer window into how Canada's PR admissions are actually tracking against both the official targets and the supplementary initiatives that sit outside them.

Hundreds of thousands of Indian nationals in Canada's PR pipeline — including Express Entry and PNP candidates — directly benefit from IRCC's transparency push and the in-Canada workers initiative targeting temporary residents transitioning to PR.
